guide.title: Unit 5: Political Participation: review guide
guide.intro: This unit covers who votes and why, how parties and interest groups link citizens to government, how elections and campaign finance work, and how the media shape politics. The required document here is Federalist No. 10; the required case is Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010), and Baker v. Carr (1962) and Shaw v. Reno (1993) bear on districting.

sections.title: Voting rights and turnout
body: Voting rights expanded through amendments and laws: the Fifteenth Amendment (race), the Nineteenth (sex), the Twenty-Fourth (poll taxes in federal elections), and the Twenty-Sixth (age 18), plus the Voting Rights Act of 1965, which banned literacy tests and required federal approval of voting changes in some areas.

Models of voting include rational-choice voting (based on self-interest), retrospective voting (judging past performance), prospective voting (predicting future performance), and party-line voting. Turnout is higher among older, more educated, and wealthier citizens and in presidential years; registration rules, voter ID laws, and early voting can raise or lower it.
points: Match each amendment to the group it protected.
Turnout differs by age, education, income, and type of election.

sections.title: Parties and interest groups
body: Political parties mobilize voters, nominate candidates, and organize government. Parties adapt through critical elections and realignments. Third parties struggle because of winner-take-all, single-member district elections, ballot-access rules, and the tendency of major parties to adopt popular third-party ideas.

Interest groups lobby officials, file amicus briefs, mobilize members, and fund campaigns. Madison's Federalist No. 10 argued that the causes of faction can't be removed without destroying liberty, so a large republic must control faction's effects. Groups face the free-rider problem: people can enjoy a group's gains without joining, so groups offer selective benefits to members.
points: Know at least two barriers to third parties.
Connect interest groups to Madison's argument about faction.

sections.title: Elections, money, and media
body: Presidents are chosen by the Electoral College: 538 electors, with 270 needed to win; most states give all their electors to the statewide winner. In Congress, incumbents usually win reelection thanks to name recognition, fundraising, and districts drawn by state legislatures, sometimes through partisan gerrymandering.

The Bipartisan Campaign Reform Act of 2002 limited soft money to national parties. Citizens United v. FEC (2010) held that political spending by corporations, associations, and unions is protected speech, which helped give rise to super PACs that may spend without limit if they don't coordinate with candidates. The media act as gatekeepers and scorekeepers; horse-race coverage focuses on who is ahead, and partisan and social media can deepen polarization.
points: Know what Citizens United decided and one consequence.
Incumbency advantage is especially strong in the House.

example.prompt: Explain one reason third-party candidates rarely win seats in Congress.
example.solution: Members are elected in single-member districts where the candidate with the most votes wins, so voters often avoid “wasting” votes on a third-party candidate, and the two major parties win nearly every seat.

misconceptions: “Citizens United allowed unlimited direct donations to candidates.”
It protected independent spending; limits on direct contributions to candidates remain.
“The popular vote winner always becomes president.”
The Electoral College decides, and the two can differ.
“Interest groups and political parties are the same.”
Parties run candidates for office; interest groups try to influence policy.
Registration rules, election timing, and other barriers also affect turnout.

passages.title: Source B: James Madison, Federalist No. 10, 1787
text: “By a faction, I understand a number of citizens, whether amounting to a majority or a minority of the whole, who are united and actuated by some common impulse of passion, or of interest, adversed to the rights of other citizens, or to the permanent and aggregate interests of the community. There are two methods of curing the mischiefs of faction: the one, by removing its causes; the other, by controlling its effects. . . . The latent causes of faction are thus sown in the nature of man”
passages.attribution: James Madison, writing as “Publius” to urge New York to ratify the Constitution. Public domain. Wording follows the text printed in OpenStax American Government 4e, Appendix C.
passages.licenseOrRights: The original text is in the public domain (published in 1787). StudySprint quotes it as printed in OpenStax American Government 4e (openstax.org/books/american-government-4e/pages/c-federalist-papers-10-and-51); no OpenStax commentary is copied.

questions.prompt: According to Source A, which age group had the highest turnout in the midterm election?
choices: Ages 65 and older
Ages 30–44
Ages 18–29
Ages 45–64
questions.explanation: Turnout among those 65 and older was 61%, the highest of the four groups.
choiceExplanations: Ages 30–44 turned out at 38% in the midterm.
Ages 18–29 turned out at 24%, the lowest.
Ages 45–64 turned out at 52% in the midterm.

questions.prompt: Which pattern does Source A show for every age group?
choices: Turnout was lower in the midterm election than in the presidential election
Turnout was the same in both elections for each age group of voters
Turnout was higher in the midterm election than in the presidential election
Turnout was lower among older voters than among younger voters in both
questions.explanation: Each group's midterm turnout is below its presidential turnout.
choiceExplanations: The figures differ for every group.
Every midterm figure is lower, not higher.
Older groups turned out at higher rates in both elections.

questions.prompt: Which constitutional amendment made it possible for the youngest group in Source A to vote in every state?
choices: The Nineteenth Amendment, which barred denying the vote by sex
The Twenty-Sixth Amendment, which lowered the voting age to 18
The Twenty-Fourth Amendment, which banned poll taxes in federal elections
The Fifteenth Amendment, which barred denying the vote by race
questions.explanation: The Twenty-Sixth Amendment (1971) set the voting age at 18 in all elections.
choiceExplanations: The Nineteenth Amendment concerns sex, not age.
The Twenty-Fourth Amendment concerns poll taxes, not age.
The Fifteenth Amendment concerns race, not age.

questions.prompt: What is a limitation of Source A for explaining why turnout differs by age?
choices: It reports turnout only for citizens who were under the age of 30
It doesn't show turnout for any group in a presidential election year
It can't show whether age itself, or factors such as income, causes the differences
It shows numbers of voters rather than the percentages of eligible citizens who voted
questions.explanation: Older citizens also tend to have higher incomes and longer residence, so the table alone can't isolate the effect of age.
choiceExplanations: The table covers all four age groups.
The table includes presidential-year turnout for every group.
The table reports percentages of eligible citizens.

questions.prompt: Madison defines a faction in Source B as
choices: a state government that refuses to obey the national government
citizens united by a shared interest or passion that threatens others' rights
a group of judges who share the same view of the Constitution
a political party that has won control of both houses of Congress and the presidency
questions.explanation: Madison's faction is any group, majority or minority, united by a passion or interest adverse to others' rights or the community's interests.
choiceExplanations: Madison's definition concerns citizens, not state governments.
Madison's definition concerns citizens, not judges.
Madison's definition doesn't mention parties controlling Congress.

questions.prompt: Madison writes that the causes of faction are “sown in the nature of man.” This suggests that he believed
choices: faction will disappear once the Constitution is ratified by the states and put into effect
faction can't be removed without destroying liberty, so its effects must be controlled
government should outlaw groups that form around a shared interest
only small, direct democracies can protect citizens from faction
questions.explanation: Because faction grows from human nature, Madison concludes the cure lies in controlling its effects, through a large republic.
choiceExplanations: Madison expects faction to persist, not disappear.
Outlawing groups would destroy the liberty Madison wants to protect.
Madison argues that a large republic, not a small democracy, controls faction best.

questions.prompt: Many interest groups compete to influence policy, and no single group dominates. This modern pattern best reflects
choices: elite theory, which sees power held by a small wealthy group
rational-choice voting, which sees voters acting in self-interest
pluralist theory, which sees competing groups as checking one another
participatory theory, which sees ordinary citizens deciding policy directly
questions.explanation: Pluralists argue that competition among many groups prevents any one faction from dominating, much as Madison hoped.
choiceExplanations: Elite theory claims a small group dominates.
Rational-choice voting describes individual voters, not group competition.
Participatory theory concerns direct citizen participation.
questions.licenseOrRights: Original question written for StudySprint. The unit's title and topics come from the linked College Board course page and the course's Course and Exam Description, as recorded in StudySprint's course outline (checked 2026-11-14); they were used only to confirm scope.

questions.prompt: Which modern feature of American politics best reflects Madison's goal of “controlling its effects”?
choices: A large republic in which many competing groups make it hard for one to dominate
Elections in which only property owners are allowed to vote
Rules that require all citizens to join the same political party
Laws that ban interest groups from contacting or lobbying any members of Congress
questions.explanation: Madison argued that a large republic multiplies interests so no faction can easily form a dangerous majority.
choiceExplanations: Property requirements limit participation; they aren't Madison's cure.
Forced party membership would destroy liberty.
Banning groups attacks faction's causes by limiting liberty, which Madison rejects.

questions.prompt: The Fifteenth Amendment (1870) prohibits denying the right to vote on the basis of
choices: age
wealth
sex
race
questions.explanation: The Fifteenth Amendment bars denying the vote because of race, color, or previous condition of servitude.
choiceExplanations: Age was addressed by the Twenty-Sixth Amendment (1971).
Poll taxes in federal elections were banned by the Twenty-Fourth Amendment (1964).
Sex was addressed by the Nineteenth Amendment (1920).

questions.prompt: The Voting Rights Act of 1965 increased Black voter registration mainly by
choices: lowering the voting age for national elections from twenty-one years old to eighteen years
creating the Electoral College system for choosing the president of the country
requiring all states to hold primary elections for congressional nominations
banning literacy tests and requiring federal approval of voting changes in some areas
questions.explanation: The act banned literacy tests and required certain jurisdictions to get federal approval before changing voting rules.
choiceExplanations: The voting age was lowered by the Twenty-Sixth Amendment.
The Electoral College was created by the Constitution.
The act didn't require primary elections.

questions.prompt: A voter decides to vote against the president's party because the economy did poorly over the past four years. This is an example of
choices: party-line (straight-ticket) voting
prospective voting
retrospective voting
ticket splitting
questions.explanation: Judging officials by their past performance is retrospective voting.
choiceExplanations: Party-line voting means voting for one party regardless of performance.
Prospective voting is based on predictions of future performance.
Ticket splitting means voting for different parties on one ballot.

questions.prompt: Which is a main function of political parties?
choices: Nominating candidates and mobilizing voters
Writing regulations for federal agencies
Appointing judges to the federal courts
Interpreting the meaning of the Constitution
questions.explanation: Parties recruit and nominate candidates, mobilize voters, and organize government.
choiceExplanations: Agencies write regulations.
The president appoints judges with Senate consent.
Interpreting the Constitution is the courts' role.

questions.prompt: Which feature of American elections most discourages third-party candidates?
choices: Laws that bar third-party members from voting
Winner-take-all elections in single-member districts
The Constitution's ban on parties other than two
Supreme Court rulings that outlawed most minor parties
questions.explanation: When only the top vote-getter wins, voters avoid “wasting” votes on candidates unlikely to win.
choiceExplanations: No law bars third-party members from voting.
The Constitution doesn't mention political parties.
The Court hasn't outlawed minor parties.

questions.prompt: When an interest group files an amicus curiae brief, it is
choices: donating money directly to a candidate's campaign committee
nominating its own candidate to run for a seat in Congress
asking voters to sign a petition to put a measure on the ballot
presenting arguments to a court in a case it isn't a party to
questions.explanation: An amicus (“friend of the court”) brief offers a court arguments from an outside group.
choiceExplanations: Campaign donations are a different tactic.
Interest groups don't nominate candidates; parties do.
Ballot petitions are part of direct democracy, not court cases.

questions.prompt: Many people who benefit from an interest group's work never join it. To overcome this free-rider problem, groups often
choices: ask Congress to require every citizen to join at least one interest group
refuse to tell the public which policies they are trying to influence
stop working on any issue that would also benefit people who aren't members
offer selective benefits, such as magazines or discounts, only to members
questions.explanation: Benefits available only to members give people a reason to join and pay dues.
choiceExplanations: No law requires membership in interest groups.
Secrecy doesn't solve the free-rider problem.
Groups keep pursuing broad goals; selective benefits supplement them.

questions.prompt: How many electoral votes does a presidential candidate need to win the election?
questions.explanation: A majority of the 538 electoral votes, 270, is required.
choiceExplanations: 51 is a majority of the Senate.
538 is the total number of electors.
218 is a majority of the House of Representatives.

questions.prompt: Which factor best explains why members of the House of Representatives usually win reelection?
choices: Incumbents' name recognition, fundraising, and favorable districts
A constitutional rule that gives incumbents extra votes in a primary
Term limits that prevent strong challengers from running for the seat
The requirement that challengers be approved by the sitting member
questions.explanation: Incumbents enjoy visibility, campaign money, constituent service, and districts often drawn to favor them.
choiceExplanations: No such rule exists.
There are no term limits for members of Congress.
Challengers need no approval from incumbents.

questions.prompt: Citizens United v. Federal Election Commission (2010) held that
choices: all campaign contributions must be disclosed within a day
corporations may give unlimited money directly to candidates
the Federal Election Commission may ban most political advertising
political spending by corporations and unions is protected speech
questions.explanation: The Court ruled that independent political spending by corporations, associations, and unions is protected by the First Amendment, which helped lead to super PACs.
choiceExplanations: The case didn't create a one-day disclosure rule.
Limits on direct contributions to candidates remain in place.
The ruling limited, rather than expanded, the government's power to restrict political ads.

questions.prompt: News coverage that focuses mainly on which candidate is ahead in the polls is known as
choices: a free-rider problem
horse-race journalism
investigative journalism
a gerrymander
questions.explanation: Horse-race coverage treats elections like a race, emphasizing polls and strategy over issues.
choiceExplanations: The free-rider problem concerns interest group membership.
Investigative journalism uncovers hidden wrongdoing.
A gerrymander is a district drawn to favor a party or group.

questions.prompt: Which development has most likely contributed to political polarization in recent decades?
choices: The requirement that senators be elected directly by the voters of each state
The decision in Marbury v. Madison that established the Supreme Court's power of judicial review
The growth of partisan media and social media that let people hear mainly views they share
The adoption of the Twenty-Sixth Amendment, which lowered the voting age to eighteen
questions.explanation: Choosing news sources that confirm existing views can harden partisan divisions, sometimes called echo chambers.
choiceExplanations: Direct election of senators dates from 1913.
Marbury dates from 1803 and concerns judicial power.
Lowering the voting age expanded participation; it isn't linked to recent polarization in this way.
